content.title: 63 at 40: Why Augusta National course record refuses to be broken
content.text: Sign up for our daily newsletter Latest news, reviews, analysis and opinion, plus unmissable deals for bunkered subscriptions, events, and our commercial partners. Thank you for signing up! While course records around the world continue to tumble, the number at the Masters is staying strong. It has been 40 years since we last saw the tournament’s record number broken. The man to do so was Nick Price, who carded a nine-under-par 63 in the third round in 1986. Ten years later, this was matched by Greg Norman – “matched” being the operative word. Thirty years on from Norman’s record-equalling effort, the number remains in tact, and hasn’t been touched since. In 2016, three decades after setting the record, Price was left baffled as to why it still stood. “It’s a mystery,” he said. “I don’t understand it.” Price went on to declare that he expected his time as course record-holder to come soon come to an end, especially considering the way the modern golfer competes. The Zimbabwean has a point. The sheer power the current crop of players possess has seen some of golf’s most iconic venues succumb to the ever-changing evolution of the pro game. Not at Augusta National, though. In the ten years since Price’s comments back in 2016, there have been 2,907 scores recorded at The Masters, none of them better than 64. • The Masters: Rory McIlroy shows a side to him that Augusta has never seen before • My first walk around Augusta: It was like stepping onto a movie set Even then, only five rounds have come within one of Price and Norman’s record, but why? Who better to ask than a past champion. Charl Schwartzel knows exactly what it takes to tame the Augusta beast, but he believes little changes each year are protecting Price and Norman’s record. “They keep lengthening the course,” he explained. “They keep staying up with the technology. They’re always changing something. And then it’s also the Masters. It’s not so easy to shoot 63.” It’s a fair point. This year, Augusta National is 130 yards longer than it was when Schwartzel won his Green Jacket in 2011, and 660 yards longer than it was when Price set the mark 40 years ago. This, combined with hitting into notoriously slick greens, is why former world No. 1 Jason Day believes the course record is safe for the foreseeable future. “Now that they’ve lengthened the holes, it’s definitely a lot harder to birdie some of them,” Day said. “You come in with longer clubs and the greens are still firm and fast. “It is very rare, unless it’s like perfect conditions where there’s just been some downpour and they’re very receptive. You’ll get your 64, 65 once a tournament here, but I don’t think you’ll see the course record broken anytime soon.” One man who flirted with the long-standing record was a fresh-faced Anthony Kim back in 2009. Playing in the second round, Kim did break one of Price’s records, making 11 birdies for the first time across 18 holes at the Masters, surpassing Price’s tally of ten during his 63. Despite birdies en masse, Kim still could not get to that magic number, as a bogey and a double ended his chances. Justin Rose went through similar during last year’s final round. • The 8 best players never to have won The Masters • The Masters: Every LIV Golf player in the 2026 Masters One of his best Masters showings came on the final day in 2025, where he shot a 66 to force a playoff with Rory McIlroy. Rose’s rise through the pack that Sunday was incredible, but as Kim encountered 16 years ago, blemishes on your card around this course are hard to avoid. “If you’re on and it’s your day, you’re going to make a lot of birdies, but you’re also going to make a bogey or two quite easily,” Rose said. “That was the nature of my round on Sunday [last year]. Made a lot of birdies, played great; still made some mistakes. This course can do that to you pretty easily.” Rose, too, conceded that the lengthening of the golf course has more than played a part, despite being left somewhat surprised that the record has stood for so long amid the calibre of player than arrive on site every year. Could we finally see the number broken this week? With fast and firm conditions expected come Thursday, it will take something very special to do just that. Josh Lees is a Content Producer at bunkered and joined the team in August 2025. Formerly of The Mirror, he covers all aspects of the game, from breaking tour news to in depth features. A member of Brookdale Golf Club in Manchester, Josh finds himself on the blue side of the city's footballing divide and is Pep Guardiola's biggest fan.
